title: My family
title_target: គ្រួសារខ្ញុំ — kruè-saa khnyom
goal: Name your family members and their ages — and discover that Khmer uses the words for "older sibling" and "younger sibling" as pronouns, for "you" and even for "I".
bekal: name the members of your immediate family
use បង and ប្អូន as "you" AND as "I"
ask someone's age with អាយុប៉ុន្មាន?
show possession without any linking word
ask how many people with ប៉ុន្មាននាក់?

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — Looking at family photos
dialogs.intro: Sreymom takes out her phone and shows a photo of her family. Notice how the two of them refer to themselves: Sreymom, the younger, uses ប្អូន; Ani, the older, uses បង. In several lines there is no ខ្ញុំ at all — and the sentences are still polite, even warmer.

grammars.title: ⚠️ បង and ប្អូន — family words used as pronouns
body: This is the point that trips English speakers up for months. In Khmer you address other people — and refer to yourself — with **kinship words**, not with "I" and "you". Imagine saying "Does big sister want some tea?" to a waitress, and "Little brother will come too" about yourself. That is everyday, polite Khmer.
after: ⚠️ What matters is not blood relation but **the age gap you estimate**. You call a café waiter បង if he looks older than you, and ប្អូន if younger. Guessing wrong is no big deal; avoiding it altogether by always using អ្នក is what sounds cold.

Look at lines 10 and 12 of the dialogue: Ani calls herself បង, not ខ្ញុំ, because she is the older one. Her sentence literally says "big sister has an older sister" — and that is completely natural. When in doubt, ខ្ញុំ is never wrong.

grammars.title: Possession without a linking word
body: The order is **thing first, owner second**, with nothing in between. There is no equivalent of "my", "of", or 's: "house I" simply means "my house".

rows: គ្រួសារប្អូន
សៀវភៅរបស់ខ្ញុំ

after: របស់ (*ra-boh*) means "belonging to" and can be added when you want to stress ownership, especially of things. For people — father, mother, family — Cambodians almost never use it. ⚠️ Using របស់ for family members sounds as if you own them.

grammars.title: Age, number of people, and ប៉ុន្មាន
body: ប៉ុន្មាន (*pon-maan*) means "how many, how much", and it stands **after** the thing being asked about.

head: English
Khmer
Say it
rows: អាយុប៉ុន្មាន?
ប៉ុន្មាននាក់?
ថ្លៃប៉ុន្មាន?

after: ⚠️ There is no "am": ខ្ញុំអាយុ ២៩ ឆ្នាំ is literally "I age 29 year". អាយុ itself is the Sanskrit *āyus*, "lifespan" — the same root as *Ayurveda*.

នាក់ (*neak*) is the classifier for people — "five persons", not just "five". Leaving it out sounds like saying "five" without saying five of what. English does something similar with "five head of cattle"; Khmer does it with people every time.

English
rows: ប្អូនប្រុស
កូនប្រុស / កូនស្រី
ប្តី / ប្រពន្ធ

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice the recurring pattern: ប្រុស (*proh*, male) and ស្រី (*srey*, female) are attached **after** the base word to show gender: "sibling-older male" = older brother. Once you know បង and ប្អូន, you automatically know four words.

blocks.title: Why people ask your age on day one
items: **Age decides the form of address.** Cambodians need to know whether you are older or younger to choose between បង and ប្អូន. "How old are you?" is not small talk and not at all rude — it is a grammar question.
**If you'd rather not give a number**, answer ជិតៗគ្នា (*chit-chit knie*, "about the same age") with a smile. That settles the matter.
**Age is counted from birth, as in the West.** Unlike Korea or parts of China, no extra year is added.
